title: Apps, Plugins and Functions: Extensibility and Ecosystem Governance
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/31-extensibility-and-app-ecosystems/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Modalities, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter, plus the units the contract asks for that the published chapter did not have: a roadmap p05 and a conclusion paragraph p49 that answers the opening; see decision_log.

know: The five ways to extend a platform (in-process plugins, theme code, apps over APIs with scopes, functions, synchronous call-outs), placed by where they run, what they may touch and how tightly they are tied to the vendor's releases, with dated vendor examples.
The app store as a business and as governance: what review checks (least scope, performance, clean uninstall, privacy webhooks) and what it cannot see.
The Forked Platform and its hosted mirror: upgrade cost and the vendor's support clock (Adobe), and extension points withdrawn on announced dates (Shopify's checkout template and Scripts).
believe: App review protects the platform and the shopper; which app may write stock or prices is the merchant's decision, and no vendor can make it.
One writer per fact: set and adjust do not mix on one number.
A platform the merchant cannot upgrade is a platform it has already left; custom behavior belongs on the lowest rung that works, never in the core.
can_do: Place any extension on the mechanism table and say which failure it risks.
Run the one-writer-per-fact test on their own app list, and write an app governance card with owner, scopes, API version and support end, review date and exit plan.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given two apps writing one stock figure, the reader explains why review did not catch it and names the merchant's governance, not a better app.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand finds the stock shown on its storefront drifting away from its warehouse count. The warehouse feed sets each variant's stock every hour; a pre-order app subtracts pre-ordered quantities from the same number; both passed the platform's app review. Using only this chapter: why did review not catch this, and what should the brand change?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Each app passed review alone and asked for its write scope for a reason; review cannot know which system owns stock in this business. Setting and adjusting one number make it drift from both. One writer per fact (the warehouse feed, later an availability service), the pre-order app's write scope revoked and pre-orders held in their own state; an owner, scopes and API version on a card per app; a reconciliation job comparing the platform with the warehouse; a quarterly uninstall review.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what risk deep customization carries on a self-run platform and on a hosted one, and how each is managed.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: one merchant runs an open-source or suite platform with years of custom modules in the core; another runs a hosted platform with checkout customizations built on the vendor's extension points. What risk does each carry, and how is it managed?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The first is the Forked Platform: in-process code ties every upgrade to the core, upgrade cost grows with the number and quality of modules, and the vendor's support clock turns a postponed upgrade into a forced migration (Adobe stops maintaining cloud environments on unsupported versions from 1 June 2027); manage the module count, an upgrade calendar and moving logic out of process. The second carries deprecation risk: hosted platforms withdraw extension points on announced dates (Shopify's checkout template in August 2024, Scripts in June 2026); record which date each app depends on and move before it. One app inventory manages both.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say where a new custom behavior should be built.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: the business asks for a behavior the platform does not have. Where should it be built?
acceptance_criteria.expected: On the lowest rung that works: configuration first, then a platform extension point (a function, call-out or workflow), then a public app for a commodity capability, then a custom app with a named owner and a pinned API version; an in-process plugin only rarely, where synchronous control of the core is needed; an edit to the core never.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why installing an app for a missing feature also decides which business facts another program may control; how two extensions changing the same fact (a pre-order app and a warehouse feed) make availability unreliable, and why permissions and an owner are assigned at installation; Kestrel & Pine's 41 apps, 6 unused and 3 writing stock, and the April 2027 ownership rule; Eva's product page with a size guide, stock badge and reviews; how platforms let other code change them, what each mechanism may touch, why apps sprawl and how to govern them. Evidence: vendors' documentation and Kestrel & Pine's app inventory.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the draft, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as sections[].paragraphs[].

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture; most of all the engineer or product manager who inherits a platform with dozens of installed apps and an agency that installed half of them (Milan Petrov and Noor Visser at Kestrel & Pine); next, the leader who approves app installs and agency work.

Kestrel & Pine, its people, its 2026 and January 2027 incidents in outline, the sixteen failure-pattern names and the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines, 'system', 'the shop platform' for the hosted product and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems, the four scale stages (Starting, Growing, Omnichannel, Group), the capability map, bounded context, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and order management system, availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.

From Parts II to VI: available-to-promise with one writer each for on hand and committed; checkout creating the order once; an integration style per flow with an owner, a reconciliation job, pinned API versions and sunset dates.

From chapters 29 and 30: the vendor's inside versus the merchant's own layer; pooled tenants kept apart by the vendor; rate limits per app and store that the vendor may lower, spent mostly by apps and connectors.

The Forked Platform and the Pulled Rug as named failures.

thesis.question: How do platforms let merchants and partners extend them without breaking them, and how should a merchant govern its apps?
thesis.claim: Platforms bound extensions by where code runs: an in-process plugin can reach the core's code and data and ties every upgrade to it; an app reaches only its granted scopes on a dated API version; a function gets a fixed input, output and time budget. App review cannot see two apps writing one business fact, so the merchant governs: an owner, scopes and API version per app, one writer per fact such as stock or price.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the app store's review keeps installed apps safe, so a merchant may install whatever the business asks for, let its agency add apps as needed, and modify the platform's core or theme when no app fits.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim keeps a card per app (owner, scopes, API version and support end, review date, exit plan), names one writer per fact and revokes every other write scope on it, runs a quarterly uninstall review, and puts custom behavior on the lowest rung that works. In March 2026 Kestrel & Pine's warehouse feed set stock every hour while a pre-order app adjusted it, giving two weeks of phantom reservations on 600 variants. The April 2027 inventory found 41 apps (about €2,900 a month, illustrative), 6 unused and 3 able to write inventory; the May 2027 reconciliation found 2.3% of active variants with a different quantity, most from those apps. Under the governance rule approved that April, the 6 were uninstalled, write access was withdrawn from the 3 by June 2027, and 34 apps remained in July at about €2,400 a month.
thesis.how_why: The deeper extension code sits, the more it can touch and the more each vendor release can break it: an in-process module must stay compatible with every core version, the vendor's support clock turns a postponed upgrade into a forced migration, and hosted platforms retire extension points on dates they announce. Each app passes review alone and asks for the write scope its job needs; which system owns stock or price is a decision about the merchant's business that no vendor sees, so an app that sets a number and another that adjusts it both work while the number drifts from both. Only the merchant's own list of owners, scopes and writers connects them.

supporting_claims.claim: Extension mechanisms differ by where the code runs, what it may touch and how tightly it is tied to the vendor's releases: an in-process plugin reaches the core's code and data and ties every upgrade to it, an app reaches only its granted scopes on a dated API version, and a function or call-out gets a fixed input, a fixed output and a time budget.

App review, scopes and dated API versions protect the platform and the shopper, but no review can see two installed apps writing one business fact, because which system owns a fact is a decision about the merchant's business.
One writer per fact: set and adjust do not mix on one number, so each fact the platform holds has one system of record and one path that writes it, and every other write scope on it is revoked.

Deep customization ties the merchant to the core: upgrade cost grows with in-process modules until the vendor's support clock forces a migration, while hosted platforms retire extension points on announced dates; custom behavior therefore goes on the lowest rung that works and never into the core.

Governance is the merchant's own inventory: an owner, scopes, API version and support end per app on a card, one writer per fact and a quarterly uninstall review, sized to the scale stage; Kestrel & Pine went from 41 apps, 6 unused and 3 writing stock, to 34 apps with no app writing stock.

role.contribution: Governs the spenders of the merchant's budget and the code that changes its platform: the five extension mechanisms placed by what they may touch and how they age, what app review does and does not protect, the one-writer-per-fact rule, the app governance card and the ladder for where custom behavior lives.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene to in-practice: Noor's question, then the rule that answers it

flow.rationale: The scene comes first so every later section answers part of Noor's question. The five mechanisms come next because every later section uses their terms (scope, extension point, in process); the app store follows because review is the vendor's answer to the risks the mechanisms carry and its gap is the merchant's problem; the writer section follows the gap because it states the rule that closes it; the Forked Platform follows because it turns from code that writes facts to code that changes the platform itself; the ladder then places custom behavior using both risks; the stage table, Kestrel & Pine's rule and the failures apply all of it, in the book's fixed order. Putting the writer rule before the app store would give a rule for a gap the reader has not seen; putting the ladder before the Forked Platform would recommend rungs before the reader knows why the lower ones cost more; putting the mechanisms after the scene's question unanswered for long would be worse than the reverse, because the question needs the terms.

hook.content: A merchant needs a size guide, a pre-order flow or a loyalty scheme its platform does not provide; an app adds it quickly, but to do its job the app may need customer records or permission to change prices and stock, so choosing the feature also decides which business facts another program may control.

bridge.to_topic: The step from that click to the chapter's question: what each kind of extension may touch, and who in the merchant decides which program writes stock, prices or orders.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: Forty-One Apps and One Spreadsheet
sections.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine's April 2027 app inventory found 41 apps that few people knew, 6 unused and 3 able to write stock beside the warehouse feed, and nobody who decided which program could write stock.

advances_thesis.how: Sets the case the governance rule answers: an unowned app list with three extra writers of stock.

flow.rationale: From the whole list and its cost, to the three apps that write stock, to the one incident, to the question the chapter answers; the question would mean nothing before the reader has seen the three writers.

transition_in.carries_over: The introduction's 41 apps, 6 unused and 3 writing stock, and Noor's April 2027 rule.
transition_in.introduces: The April 2027 inventory that produced those figures.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In April 2027 Noor and Milan inventoried all 41 apps: Milan knew about twenty well, the agency had installed 22 over several years, and the rest came from campaigns, pilots and former staff.

evidence.what: 41 installed apps; 22 installed by the agency; Milan knows about twenty well.
evidence.shows: Shows an app list nobody owns as a whole.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Recording each app's purpose, owner and permissions, not only counting the apps, is what let Noor find the unused subscriptions and the apps that write the same facts.

evidence.what: About €2,900 a month (illustrative) across platform and agency invoices and three company cards.
evidence.shows: The cost nobody could account for app by app.

evidence.what: The 41 apps by category, with unused apps, apps that write platform data and an example per category (illustrative breakdown).

sections.heading: Five Ways to Extend a Platform
sections.controlling_idea: Platforms let other code in through five mechanisms, and where each runs, what it may touch and how tightly it is tied to the vendor's releases decide how dangerous it is.

advances_thesis.how: Places each mechanism by the three tests, with the vendors' own documentation.

additional_patterns.applies_to: p14 to p20: from the deepest mechanism (in process) to the most bounded (functions and call-outs)

flow.rationale: Why extensions exist, then the three tests, then the table of five mechanisms, then each mechanism from the one that reaches furthest to the most bounded, then the common design and what each interaction needs; the summary rule about extension points would be empty before the reader has seen the bounded mechanisms.

transition_in.carries_over: Noor's question: who may let a program write stock.
transition_in.introduces: How platforms let programs in at all, the first thing needed to answer it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Answering Noor's question starts with how programs get into a platform: extensions let a shared platform serve different businesses without a separate core for each, which is why hosted platforms run one version for every merchant and list thousands of apps.

evidence.what: Shopify 10-K FY2025: 'single branch' software, 'millions' of merchants, 'more than 21,000 apps'; SAP Commerce 'a flexible, modular architecture based on extensions'.
evidence.shows: Shows extensibility as the design of shared platforms at two scales.
evidence.source: Shopify 10-K, filed 11 February 2026; SAP Help Portal

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Three things decide how dangerous an extension is: where it runs, what it may touch (everything, or only the data its permissions, called scopes, cover) and how tightly it is coupled to the platform's version.

transition_in.carries_over: Many extensions on one shared platform.
transition_in.introduces: The three tests that tell them apart.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An extension point is a named place in the platform's flow where it agrees to run or call someone else's code, and platforms offer five kinds.

evidence.what: Five mechanisms (in-process plugin, theme code, app over APIs and webhooks, serverless function, synchronous call-out) by where they run, what they can touch, version coupling and dated examples.
evidence.shows: Places each mechanism on the three tests at once.

transition_in.carries_over: The three tests.
transition_in.introduces: The term 'extension point' and the five mechanisms placed on the tests.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An in-process plugin runs inside the platform program and can do anything it can, including replacing the platform's own logic, and several plugins can disagree about which runs first.

evidence.what: Adobe Commerce plugins: before, after, around; sortOrder; around plugins 'should be avoided unless they're required'.
evidence.shows: The vendor's own description of how deep an in-process plugin reaches.
evidence.source: Adobe Commerce PHP developer guide, accessed November 2026

transition_in.carries_over: The table's first row.
transition_in.introduces: The in-process plugin explained.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Vendors that offer in-process code warn about upgrades and draw the line themselves: a vendor that runs the platform for you cannot let your code run inside it.

evidence.what: WooCommerce: backwards compatibility 'is not guaranteed'; Salesforce: 'you never edit app_storefront_base directly'; Shopware: plugins 'have direct access to the database' and 'are not supported by Shopware cloud'.
evidence.shows: Three vendors stating the cost and limit of in-process code.
evidence.source: WooCommerce, Salesforce Trailhead, Shopware documentation, accessed November 2026

transition_in.carries_over: Adobe's description of plugins.
transition_in.introduces: Three more vendors' warnings and Shopware's line between plugins and apps.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Theme code is a second place where outside code lands, and hand-edited theme files carry the risk the chapter later names the Forked Platform, glossed here as a platform changed so deeply it cannot be upgraded: every theme update becomes a merge.

evidence.what: Shopify Online Store 2.0 (29 June 2021): theme app extensions introduced to end 'ghost code' left by uninstalled apps.
evidence.shows: Shows apps injecting code into themes and the vendor's fix.

transition_in.carries_over: Code inside the platform's program.
transition_in.introduces: Code inside the storefront renderer.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An app is a separate program that talks to the platform through its APIs and webhooks and may do only what its granted scopes allow.

evidence.what: Shopify scopes read_inventory, write_inventory, read_orders, write_orders; order scopes cover the last 60 days unless a broader scope is approved; Saleor apps as external services.
evidence.shows: Shows what a scope is in practice.
evidence.source: Shopify access scopes; Saleor documentation, accessed November 2026

transition_in.carries_over: Code that runs inside the platform or its renderer.
transition_in.introduces: Code that runs outside and is limited by scopes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Apps are loosely coupled because the API is versioned with a support window, and the price of that looseness is an upgrade obligation for every app.

evidence.what: Shopify releases an API version every three months, supports each for at least 12 months, and 'falls forward' from a retired one.
evidence.shows: Shows the dated contract an app depends on.

transition_in.carries_over: Apps that reach the platform only through its API.
transition_in.introduces: What the versioned API gives them and what it costs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The newest mechanism runs the merchant's small program at a named moment in the platform's flow with a fixed input, a fixed output and a time limit, as Shopify Functions do, after Scripts were retired.

evidence.what: Shopify Functions: WebAssembly, JSON in, operations out, no network; limits for 2026-10 of 11 million instructions, 10 MiB memory, 256 KiB module; Scripts retired 30 June 2026.
evidence.shows: Shows how tightly a function is bounded.
evidence.source: shopify.dev Functions; Script Editor help page

transition_in.carries_over: Apps outside the process.
transition_in.introduces: Functions, which run inside the request path but in a sandbox.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A synchronous call-out lets the platform ask the merchant's endpoint before saving a change, so its latency and failures become the merchant's.

evidence.what: commercetools API Extensions: 'if it fails or takes a second longer..., the whole API call fails or takes a second longer'; 2 s budgets, about 50 ms target, 25 per project, no retry.
evidence.shows: Shows the call-out's budget and failure rule in the vendor's words.

transition_in.carries_over: Functions with a fixed input, output and time limit.
transition_in.introduces: The call-out variant of the same idea.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The common design is the lesson: an extension point is a named moment with a fixed input, a fixed output, a time budget and a failure rule, and the time budget is the vendor protecting checkout from the merchant's code.

evidence.what: Figure 1: where an extension runs decides what it can touch.
evidence.shows: Shows the three depths side by side.

transition_in.carries_over: Functions and call-outs.
transition_in.introduces: The design they share.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The five mechanisms meet in four interactions a merchant actually has (a webhook being the notification half of an app over APIs), each needing a different time budget and failure rule and someone who answers when it fails, the question the rest of the chapter takes up.

evidence.what: Checkout validation, stock write, order webhook and replaced core method, with mechanism, time budget, failure rule and owner (vendors' documented budgets; one labelled assumption).
evidence.shows: Shows the rule applied to the interactions a merchant actually has.

transition_in.carries_over: The extension point's time budget and failure rule.
transition_in.introduces: The four interactions a merchant has, with the webhook placed as part of an app over APIs and the owner column announced as the chapter's next question.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every interaction except the replaced core method has a platform rule for failure; in-process code has none, because the platform no longer knows what it is doing.

transition_in.introduces: The one row without a failure rule.

sections.heading: The Forked Platform and the Pulled Rug
sections.controlling_idea: Customizing the core makes a platform un-upgradable until the vendor's support clock forces a migration, and hosted platforms carry the mirror risk of extension points withdrawn on announced dates; one inventory manages both.

advances_thesis.how: Documents the upgrade risk and the deprecation risk in the vendors' words and dates.

flow.rationale: The definition, then Adobe's evidence in three steps (guidance, tool, its own out-of-process reasoning), then the support clock that turns the cost into a deadline, then the hosted mirror, then the comparison that joins them.

transition_in.carries_over: Apps that write facts through a platform's API.
transition_in.introduces: Code that changes the platform itself.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Set against programs working through the API, the Forked Platform is a platform whose core or theme has been customized so deeply that it can no longer be upgraded, so every release becomes a project and eventually none is taken.
Adobe's upgrade guidance says the amount and quality of custom work and third-party modules decide how hard an upgrade is, and skipped releases make the next one harder.

evidence.what: 'The amount of custom work and the number of installed third-party modules strongly affects the complexity of an upgrade'.
evidence.shows: The vendor stating the cost of in-process customization.
evidence.source: Adobe Experience League upgrade best practices, accessed November 2026

transition_in.carries_over: The Forked Platform.
transition_in.introduces: The vendor's own description of its cost.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adobe ships a tool that checks a customized instance against a target version and reports the issues, and that the vendor builds such a tool shows how common the problem is.

evidence.what: Upgrade Compatibility Tool reports 'critical issues, errors, and warnings' (updated 8 October 2026).
evidence.shows: Shows the vendor building tooling for the upgrade problem.

transition_in.carries_over: Adobe's guidance.
transition_in.introduces: Adobe's tool for the same problem.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adobe's reasoning for its out-of-process model is the same lesson from the vendor's side: in-process code must stay compatible with every version, while out-of-process apps run on their own schedule at the cost of deep synchronous control.

evidence.what: In-process code 'must stay compatible with each Commerce version and its runtime'; App Builder apps 'developed, deployed, and operated on their own schedule'.
evidence.shows: The vendor weighing coupling against control.

transition_in.carries_over: Adobe's guidance and tool.
transition_in.introduces: Adobe's reasoning for moving extensions out of process.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The vendor's support policy turns a postponed upgrade into a forced migration: about three years of standard support per release, and from 1 June 2027 cloud environments on unsupported versions are taken offline.

evidence.what: 2.4.4: GA 12 April 2022, standard support to 12 April 2025; 2.4.7: GA 9 April 2024, supported to 31 May 2027; from 1 June 2027 traffic suspended, the storefront 'will go offline'.
evidence.shows: Gives the clock dated deadlines.
evidence.source: Adobe Commerce lifecycle policy, accessed November 2026

transition_in.carries_over: Upgrade cost that grows with modules.
transition_in.introduces: The clock that turns the cost into a deadline.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Hosted platforms cannot be forked but withdraw extension points on announced dates (the book's Pulled Rug), so an extension point is a promise with a date that the merchant's inventory must record.

evidence.what: checkout.liquid stopped working 13 August 2024 by a notice of 13 February 2023, non-upgraded checkouts automatically replaced; Scripts retired 30 June 2026.
evidence.shows: Shows the hosted mirror of the upgrade risk.
evidence.source: Shopify changelog, 13 February 2023; Script Editor help page

transition_in.carries_over: Self-run platforms whose core the merchant changed.
transition_in.introduces: Hosted platforms whose extension points the vendor withdraws.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Open source and suites put the upgrade risk in the merchant's hands and hosted SaaS the deprecation risk; neither is safe, and both are managed by the same inventory.

evidence.what: Figure 3: upgrade risk beside deprecation risk, one inventory.
evidence.shows: Shows both risks managed by one list.

transition_in.carries_over: The upgrade risk and the deprecation risk.
transition_in.introduces: The two set side by side and joined by one inventory.

sections.heading: The Choices: Where Custom Behavior Should Live
sections.controlling_idea: Custom behavior belongs on the lowest rung of a ladder that works: configuration, a native extension point, a public app, a custom app with an owner, an in-process plugin rarely, the core never.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the mechanisms and their risks into a placement rule.

transition_in.carries_over: The upgrade and deprecation risks of deep customization.
transition_in.introduces: Where custom behavior should therefore go.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because both risks grow with the depth of a change, the author climbs a ladder of six places from the top and stops at the first rung that works: configuration (with Hodgson's three kinds of feature toggle glossed), a platform-native extension point, a public app, a custom app with an owner and a pinned API version, an in-process plugin only for synchronous core control, and editing the core never.

evidence.what: Six choices by upgrade coupling, what they may touch, latency risk to checkout, who maintains them and when each is right.
evidence.shows: Shows why each rung costs more than the one above.

evidence.what: Pete Hodgson, Feature Toggles (2017); Shopify Flow help page.
evidence.shows: Support the configuration and workflow rungs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The ladder assumes a small team that does not sell software: a Group-stage merchant with a platform team on a suite can afford a budgeted in-process layer, and Kestrel & Pine, with three storefront-and-apps engineers and an agency, cannot.

evidence.what: Kestrel & Pine's technology team: three storefront-and-apps engineers among nine engineers, plus the agency.
evidence.shows: Places Kestrel & Pine on the ladder's assumption.

transition_in.carries_over: The ladder as a general recommendation.
transition_in.introduces: Who it fits and who can depart from it.

sections.heading: Across Scale Stages: When It Fits and When It Limits
sections.controlling_idea: The mechanisms do not change with scale but the governance does: a list with owners and scopes from the Starting stage, a card per app and a one-writer rule at Omnichannel, a shared catalog and upgrade calendar at Group.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Extensibility is cheap to adopt and expensive to govern: the bill arrives at Omnichannel as two writers of one fact, and a list kept from the Starting stage costs almost nothing while one started at forty apps costs a week of archaeology.

sections.controlling_idea: Two dated public examples show vendors moving extensions out of the core, and Kestrel & Pine's five-line app governance rule turned the April 2027 spreadsheet into 34 owned apps with no app writing stock.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Beyond the Shopify dates already given, one dated public example shows the direction vendors are taking: Adobe's Commerce as a Cloud Service, from 2025, extends through out-of-process mechanisms rather than in-process modules.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong
sections.controlling_idea: Extensions fail the way integrations fail, often without the merchant knowing the extension exists, and every failure is found and fixed faster by a merchant that can list its apps, owners, scopes and the facts they write.

advances_thesis.how: Lists each failure with its detection and recovery.

transition_in.carries_over: Kestrel & Pine's rule working.
transition_in.introduces: The ways extensions go wrong.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Kestrel & Pine's rule works only while someone keeps it: extensions fail the way integrations fail, often without the merchant knowing the extension exists, in five ways with their own detection and recovery, two of them named the Pulled Rug (met above) and the Lynchpin (a capability that runs through one app or vendor nobody is watching). The lead also places the author's opening patterns: the first row is the Secret Agent when the writing app has no owner, and forty-one apps with their own paths into the data are the Spaghetti Junction.

evidence.what: Five failures: two writers of one fact, a lost webhook, the withdrawn extension point (the Pulled Rug), the un-upgradable core (the Forked Platform), an app as attacker's path or abandoned (the Lynchpin), with detection and recovery.
evidence.shows: Gives the reader a symptom-to-recovery map.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every failure is found and fixed faster by a merchant that can list its apps, their owners, their scopes and the facts they write.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The mechanisms, the app store and the forked core meet on one point: the platform bounds what each extension may reach, but only the merchant knows which system owns each fact, so how deep the code sits decides what an upgrade costs, while who may write each fact decides whether the shopper's promise holds. Both are answered by the same list of apps with owners, scopes, API versions and the facts they write.
conclusion.so_what: A merchant that keeps that list can answer the question Kestrel & Pine could not in March 2026, place any new behavior on the lowest rung that works, and see a deprecation or an upgrade deadline before it arrives; one that relies on app review installs the next App That Wrote Stock.

callback.to: The opening's app installed for a missing feature, Eva's jacket page with its stock badge, and Noor's question of who may let a program write stock.
callback.how: p49 answers them: installing the feature is a decision about which facts the app may write, and at Kestrel & Pine the answer is one named writer of stock, so Eva's stock badge shows a number one program sets.

takeaway.content: List every app with an owner, its scopes, its API version and support end; name one writer per fact and revoke every other write scope on it; review the list each quarter; and put custom behavior on the lowest rung that works.
